# Longevity Weekly
> **A clinical trial found daily fiber eased knee osteoarthritis pain and improved strength.**

**What You Need to Know:** A clinical trial found a daily fiber supplement eased knee osteoarthritis pain and improved strength, with researchers tying the change to gut bacteria and GLP-1. Separately, a Nature Aging paper linked statin use with a slower bone-density decline after menopause, while the bone-building mechanism it describes is experimental work in leptin-receptor-positive marrow cells. Life Biosciences also said it has interim data from a first-in-human Phase 1 reprogramming trial in three people.

### The Week in Longevity
**A simple daily fiber supplement reduced arthritis pain and improved strength: ScienceDaily Nutrition**
ScienceDaily reported a new clinical trial in which a daily fiber supplement reduced knee osteoarthritis pain, improved muscle strength, and made the body less sensitive to pain. That is a human clinical trial, not an animal study, and these sources do not establish that any regulator has approved a fiber supplement for an aging-related use. Researchers said the benefits may be linked to changes in gut bacteria and the hormone GLP-1. The write-up calls that link a promising approach to arthritis relief, which is a proposed mechanism, not proof that GLP-1 caused the pain change. Source: [sciencedaily.com](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261027230715.htm)

**Statins promote bone anabolism in estrogen deficiency by inducing osteogenic differentiation of skeletal stem/progenitor cells: Nature Aging**
Yang and colleagues, in Nature Aging, report that statin use was associated with a slower annual decline in bone mineral density in postmenopausal women, an observational association rather than a randomized trial of bone outcomes. In the same paper, atorvastatin promoted bone anabolism specifically under estrogen-deficient conditions by inducing osteogenic differentiation of leptin-receptor-expressing bone marrow stromal cells, which include skeletal stem and progenitor cells. That cell-level work is experimental: atorvastatin increased osteoblast formation by restricting RAC1 prenylation and enabling nuclear factor kappa B-mediated Oln transcription. Estrogen, the paper says, acts on the same LEPR-positive cells through estradiol–estrogen receptor-alpha signaling to promote Oln transcription, so statins are described as compensating for reduced estrogen signaling by a different route. These sources do not establish regulatory approval of statins for an aging-related bone use; the authors frame the finding as relevant beyond cholesterol management. Earlier observational studies, the paper notes, have varied across cohorts, endpoints, and designs. Source: [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43587-026-01257-1)

**Life Biosciences Announces First-in-Human Phase 1 Trial Data: Lifespan.io**
Since October 14, the open question on partial reprogramming was whether a first human trial existed; Life Biosciences has now announced interim data from a Phase 1 clinical trial of ER-100 in three participants. Lifespan.io describes the company as developing cellular rejuvenation medicines aimed at diseases of aging. A Fight Aging! newsletter the day before headed the same development as initial results from the first reprogramming trial. This is an early human trial announcement, not a published efficacy result, and these sources do not establish regulatory approval of ER-100 for any aging-related use. Source: [lifespan.io](https://lifespan.io/life-biosciences-announces-first-in-human-phase-1-trial-data/)

**Longevity expert reveals the behaviours that could add ‘15-20 years’ to your life: The Independent**
In an Independent interview, Professor Valter Longo, who heads the Longevity Institute at the University of Southern California, named a mostly plant-based pattern with some fish and little meat, a daily eating window, regular exercise, and better sleep as the low-cost actions he favors. That is expert opinion from an interview, not a new randomized human trial, and these sources do not establish that a regulator has approved a longevity diet. He said a twelve-hour eating window limits excessive eating while avoiding fasting stretches of sixteen hours or more, which he said some research associates with higher heart-disease risk. He also said his longevity diet inspired Michael Mosley’s 5:2 diet. Source: [independent.co.uk](https://www.independent.co.uk/health-and-fitness/how-to-live-longer-professor-valter-longo-b3074209.html)

**Reviewing What is Known of How the Aging Gut Microbiome May Contribute to Osteoporosis: Fight Aging!**
A Fight Aging! review describes the gut microbiome as thousands of microbial species whose balance shifts with age, with microbes that provoke chronic inflammation growing at the expense of microbes that make beneficial metabolites. The piece says researchers mapping human populations have found correlations between microbiome features, microbial metabolites, and age-related diseases, and it expects osteoporosis to have many such connections. Those are correlations discussed in a review, not a trial showing that changing the microbiome prevents fractures. Source: [fightaging.org](https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/10/reviewing-what-is-known-of-how-the-aging-gut-microbiome-may-contribute-to-osteoporosis/)

**miR-3155b is a Senomorphic MicroRNA, Reducing Senescent Cell Inflammatory Signaling: Fight Aging!**
Fight Aging! reports researchers describing miR-3155b as a senomorphic microRNA that suppresses inflammatory signaling from senescent cells, in work aimed at senescent cells left by cancer therapy. Senomorphic approaches, as that piece defines them, suppress harmful senescent-cell behavior rather than destroying the cells, which is the senolytic strategy, or slowing their creation, which is the senostatic strategy. This is a preclinical discovery report, not a human trial, and these sources do not establish regulatory approval of miR-3155b for any use. Source: [fightaging.org](https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/10/mir-3155b-is-a-senomorphic-microrna-reducing-senescent-cell-inflammatory-signaling/)

### Also Today
**Fish Oil Supplements Fail Major Test for Memory and Brain Aging: AOL.com**
AOL reported that fish oil supplements failed a major test for memory and brain aging. Source: [aol.com](https://www.aol.com/articles/fish-oil-supplements-fail-major-132200000.html)

**How Important is Lipid Metabolism Dysfunction in the Aging of Microglia?: Fight Aging!**
Fight Aging! writes that microglia become more inflammatory with age, adding to chronic brain inflammation that can disrupt function and contribute to neurodegenerative disease, and that senescence explains only some of that shift. Source: [fightaging.org](https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/10/how-important-is-lipid-metabolism-dysfunction-in-the-aging-of-microglia/)

**The Regulatory Bottleneck in Aging Biology: Lifespan.io**
Lifespan.io reports that researchers developing biomedical repair therapies meant to address several age-related diseases at once are still put through existing regulatory pathways. Source: [lifespan.io](https://lifespan.io/the-regulatory-bottleneck-in-aging-biology/)

### Mechanism of the Week: Biomarkers of Aging
In cognitively unimpaired adults, a conditional network analysis of blood inflammation markers found a CXCL5-driven network associated with age, sex, and the cerebrospinal-fluid ratio of amyloid-beta 42 to amyloid-beta 40. That study, in Neurobiology of Aging, is observational network modeling, not a treatment trial. It asked how blood inflammation markers relate directly to one another in typical aging, then split those networks into eigenvectors with hub proteins and tested the resulting eigenproteins against demographics, core Alzheimer’s biomarkers in cerebrospinal fluid and blood, and immune health history.

A biomarker of aging, in a Science China Life Sciences review, is a set of biological parameters used to assess age-related changes, track physiological aging, and predict a shift into a pathological state. The same review says an immediate use is to answer how old someone is biologically, why aging proceeds, and how aging might be slowed. It groups markers into six pillars: physiological characteristics, medical imaging, histological features, cellular alterations, molecular changes, and secretory factors. It argues a useful marker should be specific, systemic, and clinically relevant, and it says potential uses and limits of the broad existing set remain poorly characterized. That is a review framework, not a validation study.

A Cell paper from the same period of methods work says biomarkers are tools for identifying and evaluating longevity interventions in humans over realistic time frames, including as possible surrogate endpoints. It also says there is no consensus on the properties of a reliable aging biomarker, which hinders clinical validation. The authors advance a framework for terminology, classification, and potential clinical use cases, and they discuss validation steps and open challenges. A Nature Medicine review of omic biomarkers likewise says no consensus exists on how such markers should be validated before clinical translation. It reviews efforts to test predictive validity in population studies, flags problems of comparability and generalizability, and says systematic validation could speed use in gerotherapeutic trials.

The inflammation-network study shows why a single blood number is a weak stand-in for “biological age.” Networks did not all point the same way. An interleukin-6- and FGF-21-driven network was associated with sex, the cerebrospinal-fluid amyloid ratio, and Qalb, the cerebrospinal-fluid-to-serum albumin ratio, a marker tied to barrier leakiness in that paper’s outcome list. An interferon-gamma- and CXCL9-driven network was associated with both age and the cerebrospinal-fluid amyloid ratio. Networks centered on CXCL11 with CXCL9, and on CCL19 with CCL4, were associated only with sex. A network driven by MCP-3, MCP-4, and CXCL6 was associated with cumulative surgical exposures. Despite several networks tracking the cerebrospinal-fluid amyloid ratio, plasma amyloid-beta 42 to amyloid-beta 40 was not significantly associated with any blood inflammatory network. The authors’ own conclusion is that inferring immune pathophysiology from blood is both important and difficult, because inflammatory markers are pleiotropic and associate with multiple demographic and health factors at once.

A separate review in Revista de Investigación Clínica treats aging as heterogeneous: people of the same chronological age follow different biological, cognitive, and functional paths. It describes neuronal biomarkers—neuroimaging, blood-based, and neurovascular—as capturing neurodegeneration, neuroinflammation, vascular dysfunction, and impaired resilience. It describes behavioral biomarkers—gait, mobility, dual-task performance, balance, physical activity, sleep, and digital phenotyping—as the functional expression of those biological changes. The review says alterations in these markers may precede cognitive decline, frailty, disability, and loss of independence by several years. That “may precede” claim is a review of evidence, not a new measurement in a named cohort. The authors say combining neuronal markers, behavioral markers, and physical performance could identify people on adverse trajectories and support precision geroscience aimed at intrinsic capacity and functional ability. They also say multimodal models still need validation in clinical and population settings.

The oldest source in this set is a 1999 account of the Biomarkers of Aging Program, a collaboration of the National Center for Toxicological Research and the National Institute on Aging. The aim was a rodent panel that could test whether interventions slow aging, on the assumption that markers useful across genotypes and species might point to processes relevant to humans. Caloric restriction was the model of extended life span. The program generated data from over sixty thousand individually housed animals across seven mouse and rat genotypes and both sexes, about half fed ad libitum and the rest calorie-restricted. That is an animal research program, not human validation. It does not establish that a rodent marker predicts a human outcome.

What is not established is a shared pass-fail test for an aging biomarker, a regulator’s acceptance of any omic clock or blood inflammation network as a surrogate for healthspan or lifespan, and a demonstration that changing one of these networks changes dementia, frailty, or survival. The inflammation study’s limit is the sharpest finding in the set: blood networks tracked a cerebrospinal-fluid amyloid ratio and failed to track the same ratio measured in plasma, in cognitively unimpaired adults.

### Worth Knowing
- A human clinical trial found a daily fiber supplement reduced knee osteoarthritis pain and improved strength, so joint symptoms in later life are being studied as something gut signals may track, not only as local joint wear.
- In postmenopausal women, statin use was associated with a slower yearly loss of bone mineral density; that is an association, and the bone-building pathway described beside it is experimental cell work, not proof that a cholesterol drug preserves bone.
- In cognitively unimpaired adults, blood inflammation networks tracked a cerebrospinal-fluid amyloid ratio that the same study did not find in plasma amyloid, so a blood aging or Alzheimer’s marker is not automatically the same measurement as spinal fluid.
- A clinical review of aging biomarkers says changes in neuronal and behavioral markers may show up years before frailty or loss of independence, and it also says those multimodal models are not yet validated for clinic use.

### Evidence Ledger
- In cognitively unimpaired adults, blood inflammation networks showed distinct associations with age, sex, cerebrospinal-fluid amyloid ratio, albumin ratio, and surgical history, while plasma amyloid ratio was not associated with those networks; observational network analysis; https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42139770
- Aging biomarkers are parameters meant to assess age-related change, track physiological aging, and predict pathological transition, and should be specific, systemic, and clinically relevant; review; https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37076725
- There is no consensus standard for a reliable aging biomarker, which blocks clinical validation, and a terminology framework has been proposed; review; https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37657418
- No consensus exists on validating omic aging biomarkers before clinical use; population-study predictive validity is under review, with comparability problems; review; https://europepmc.org/article/MED/38355974
- Neuronal and behavioral biomarkers may precede cognitive decline, frailty, disability, and loss of independence by years, and multimodal models still need validation; review; https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42623782
- A rodent biomarkers program used caloric restriction and more than sixty thousand animals across seven genotypes to hunt markers for testing interventions meant to slow aging; animal research program; https://europepmc.org/article/MED/10619312

### Trial Tracker
- ER-100, Life Biosciences, partial cellular reprogramming candidate described as a cellular rejuvenation medicine: Phase 1, interim data announced in three participants; no next dated milestone is named in these sources.

Education only: none of this is a reason to start, stop, or change a treatment.

# Longevity Weekly
> **A tissue study of twenty-eight women found ovaries still change after menopause.**

**What You Need to Know:** A tissue study of twenty-eight women found ovaries still change after menopause. A Buck Institute and Northwestern look at ovarian tissue reported ongoing changes in proteins, inflammation, and tissue structure, and said those changes raise new questions about women's health as they age. It is a laboratory description of human tissue, not a trial of a treatment.

### The Week in Longevity
**The ovary doesn't retire after menopause: Buck Institute**
A Buck–Northwestern study of ovarian tissue from 28 women found ongoing changes in proteins, inflammation, and tissue structure after menopause. That is a laboratory study of human tissue, not a randomized trial, and it did not test a drug or a behaviour. The report says the changes raise new questions about women's health as they age. It does not describe a regulator approving any treatment on the basis of this work. Source: [buckinstitute.org](https://www.buckinstitute.org/news/the-ovary-doesnt-retire-after-menopause/)

**A dog longevity pill is nearing FDA approval. A vet explains what it can and can't do: Yahoo Creators**
Loyal, a San Francisco company, is developing LOY-002, a once-daily tablet for dogs 10 and older that weigh at least 14 pounds, and Yahoo Creators reports that the company has cleared two of the three major technical sections the FDA requires before conditional approval. The article says the pill could be available as early as late 2026 or 2027. This is a veterinary regulatory path, not an approved human aging drug, and the article does not present a published trial showing that LOY-002 itself lengthens life. Veterinarian Rebecca Greenstein told the outlet the tablet is aimed at insulin sensitivity and high insulin, with healthspan as the goal rather than freezing age. She pointed to a 14-year Purina study published in 2002, an animal feeding experiment in which Labrador retrievers fed 25 percent fewer calories than littermates stayed leaner, developed chronic disease later, and lived a median of nearly two years longer. The American Animal Hospital Association classifies 44 percent of pets as seniors. Source: [creators.yahoo.com](https://creators.yahoo.com/lifestyle/story/a-dog-longevity-pill-is-nearing-fda-approval-a-vet-explains-what-it-can-and-cant-do-174709664.html)

**1 in 4 Army Men Have Low T; GLP-1 in Menopause; Retatrutide Side Effects on Reddit: MedPage Today**
MedPage Today, citing JAMA Network Open, reported an analysis of Reddit users who said they had used retatrutide, an unapproved weight-loss drug. The most commonly cited adverse-event terms were appetite increases, fatigue, increased energy, insomnia, increases in heart rate, and muscle-related symptoms. That is an analysis of online self-reports, not a randomized trial, so it cannot establish how often those events occur or what each person actually received. No regulator has approved retatrutide for any use described in this report, including any aging-related use. Source: [medpagetoday.com](https://www.medpagetoday.com/endocrinology/generalendocrinology/123483)

**Blocking STING Helps Preserve Bone in Aging Mice: Lifespan.io**
A mouse study links STING-mediated signals from marrow fat cells to inflammation and to declining NAD+ in bone-forming cells, and interrupting that pathway helped preserve aging bone. This is an animal experiment, not a human trial. The summary does not report regulatory approval of any related approach for an aging-related use in people. Source: [lifespan.io](https://lifespan.io/blocking-sting-helps-preserve-bone-in-aging-mice/)

### Mechanism of the Week: How to Read Longevity Evidence
In 2014, Deelen and colleagues published in Human Molecular Genetics a genome-wide association study of human longevity. A commentary in Cell Cycle that year called it the largest such study to that date, and then pointed at a mismatch: genes known to extend lifespan considerably in rodents were not consistently associated with human longevity, in that scan or in genetic association studies more generally.

How to read that mismatch starts with what each design can show. A rodent experiment can show that a defined genetic change, inside a defined strain, changes lifespan or changes a pathway in tissue. A human genome-wide association study can show which variants are statistically linked to a longevity phenotype in the people enrolled. A hit in one design is not a cause proven in the other species, and neither design is a treatment test.

The commentary offers three explanations and does not pick a winner. Longevity association studies have intrinsic limits, so a large human scan can still miss a real effect. Longevity may also have a complex genetic architecture, spread across many variants, so a gene with a large effect in a mouse need not appear as a clean human hit. The author's own hypothesis is that part of the gap comes from the animal studies. Most of those studies use strains of limited genetic diversity. A result that holds in one narrow background may not apply to genetically mixed human populations. The commentary also points to other results, unnamed in the abstract, in which caloric restriction changed rodent lifespan in a strain-specific way. The upshot is a question about translation: findings from the genetics of aging may not move cleanly into human therapies. The commentary does not show that translation is impossible. It shows that the usual path from a mouse lifespan gene to a human claim is weaker than a headline implies.

 The Snell dwarf mouse carries a Pit-1 mutation. Its longevity has been associated with reduced insulin, IGF-1, and growth-hormone signaling. Those hormones, and thyroid-stimulating hormone, help set rates of protein synthesis, which decline in aged rodent tissues. Earlier work had found PI3K activity sharply lower in Snell dwarf liver. PI3K is a signaling protein that helps control translation. The 2004 study looked at young and aged Snell dwarf livers and found lower phosphorylation and lower kinase activity of Akt, also called PKB, and of p38 MAPK, and lower phosphorylation of downstream regulators of translation. The authors propose that lower protein synthesis may be an important feature of the Pit-1 mutation and of this mouse's long life. That is biochemistry in one long-lived mutant strain. It is not a human genetic association and not a randomized trial.

Set beside the commentary, those liver measurements are the kind of result that may not travel. They show lower activity at several nodes of insulin and IGF-1 signaling and of p38 MAPK signaling, and lower marks of translational initiation. A kinase reading is a molecular measurement. It is not evidence that blocking the same node would lengthen human life. The commentary's human finding is that genes with large lifespan effects in rodents have not been consistently tied to human longevity in association studies.

Several things remain unestablished. A missing association does not prove the pathway is irrelevant in people, and it does not prove the pathway matters. No paper here is a randomized human trial. Neither paper reports that a regulator has approved reduced insulin or IGF-1 signaling, p38 MAPK modulation, or any related approach for an aging-related use. Neither reports human safety results. What they do support is a limit on interpretation: a lifespan difference in a low-diversity mouse strain, or a drop in liver kinase activity, is not evidence that a therapy will work in humans.

The strongest finding on the human side is negative, and the commentary states its own limit. Rodent lifespan genes were not consistently associated with human longevity in the largest genome-wide study then available, or in association studies more generally. That gap does not say whether the biology fails in people or whether the studies were built in a way that could not show the link.

### Worth Knowing
- A laboratory study of ovarian tissue can show that menopause is not a full biological stop in that organ; it cannot show that any product changes those features.
- Symptom words people post after using an unapproved drug are a sign of use outside a trial, not a count of how often harm occurs.

### Evidence Ledger
- A 2014 commentary on the then-largest human longevity genome-wide association study found that rodent lifespan genes were not consistently associated with human longevity, and argued that limited genetic diversity in animal strains, plus strain-specific caloric-restriction effects, weakens translation to people. Evidence level: commentary on human genetic association studies and on model-organism design. Source: [europepmc.org](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/25486354)
- In Snell dwarf mouse liver, phosphorylation and kinase activity of Akt/PKB and p38 MAPK, and phosphorylation of downstream translation regulators, were decreased; the authors propose lower protein synthesis as a feature of this long-lived mutant. Evidence level: mouse tissue biochemistry. Source: [europepmc.org](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/15541773)

The useful distinction this week is between a change measured in tissue, a lifespan result in one animal strain, and a result that has actually been tied to people.

# Longevity Weekly
> **A 48% higher dementia risk tracked frequent napping in 995 older adults.**

**What You Need to Know:** In an observational follow-up of 995 older adults, frequent daytime napping tracked a 48% higher risk of later dementia. The same week brought a small human look at cellular recycling, a postmortem map of Alzheimer-linked DNA methylation, a controlled comparison of nail problems in people using GLP-1 medicines, and a mouse-and-pig muscle study. None of it is a treatment result.

### The Week in Longevity
**Frequent Daytime Napping Linked to Higher Dementia Risk in Older Adults: Mirage News**
Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health researchers followed 995 U.S. Medicare beneficiaries in an observational cohort, not a trial. Participants were 65 or older, free of dementia at the 2013 start, and were tracked for up to 10 years in the National Health and Aging Trends Study; the paper appeared online October 5 in The Journal of Gerontology: Medical Sciences. People who napped most days or every day had a 48% higher dementia risk than those who rarely or never napped, after accounting for demographics, health conditions, nighttime sleep duration, daytime sleepiness, and a measure of obstructive sleep apnea risk. Unintentional napping, falling asleep without meaning to, was linked to a 39% higher risk. Naps of 30 minutes or less were linked to a 40% higher risk, and that link held after the same confounders, while the link for naps longer than 30 minutes weakened once nighttime sleep was considered. Senior author Adam Spira said more frequent napping could be a marker of brain changes rather than a cause of them. The team describes a likely two-way relationship, because early degeneration in regions that keep a person awake may also increase napping. After dementia cases in the first five years were excluded, the frequent-napping and unintentional-napping associations remained similar. No regulator decision is attached to napping in this report. Source: [miragenews.com](https://www.miragenews.com/frequent-daytime-napping-linked-to-higher-1759538/)

**Scientists discover a surprising paradox in how our cells age: ScienceDaily**
This is a small human study of cells, reported in Aging Cell on September 27, 2026, by researchers at Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute, not a randomized trial of an aging treatment. Autophagy is the cell’s cleanup system: it packages damaged proteins and other waste and breaks them down for reuse. Senior author Caroline Kumsta said the idea that autophagy declines with age is widely cited, but the human evidence is very thin. Volunteers aged 23 to 72, all reporting no chronic medical conditions, gave blood and skin samples. Some skin cells were converted into induced neurons so the team could compare recycling in three cell types. Activity could increase, decrease, or stay the same depending on cell type and sex. The report also says a small study suggests gentle exercise may help restore more youthful recycling patterns in older adults. Interest in targeting autophagy for healthy-aging interventions is growing, lead author Tatiana Moreno said, but these sources do not describe a regulator approval for any such use. Source: [sciencedaily.com](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261012185009.htm)

**Popular weight loss drugs linked to a surprising fingernail problem: ScienceDaily**
A controlled comparison, not a randomized trial, is the first of its kind on GLP-1 medicines and nails, and it was presented at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology Congress 2026. Researchers compared 575 people using GLP-1 medications with 1,329 people who had type 2 diabetes and/or obesity and had never used the drugs, recruited in France, the United States, Brazil, and Mexico. Nail detachment was reported by 39% of users and 9% of never-users, more than four times as often. Nail discoloration affected 46% of users and 17% of never-users. At least one nail disorder was reported by 66% of users and 53% of the comparison group. The report says weight loss alone could not fully explain the differences, and its summary also links these medicines to hair loss and scalp inflammation. The named drugs, including Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound, Victoza, and Trulicity, are described as treatments for weight loss and type 2 diabetes. These sources do not report approval for slowing aging. Last week’s aging-clock claims for this drug class did not include this nail comparison. Source: [sciencedaily.com](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261011211604.htm)

**Brain DNA methylation, APOE genotype and Alzheimer’s disease neuropathology in a large postmortem cohort: Nature Aging**
A large postmortem human study, published online in Nature Aging on October 12, 2026, is an association analysis, not a clinical test and not a treatment trial. It identified 107 brain DNA methylation sites linked to Alzheimer’s pathology, and 38 of those sites were replicated independently. DNA methylation partially mediated the association between APOE genotype and an Alzheimer’s diagnosis. Methylation here is a chemical mark on DNA, measured in brain tissue after death, not a reading a clinic can act on from this paper alone. Source: [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43587-026-01243-7)

**miR-128-3p Inhibition Improves Muscle Mass and Function in Aged Mice: Fight Aging!**
This is animal evidence, summarized by Fight Aging! from a preprint, not a human trial. Antisense-oligonucleotide inhibition of miR-128-3p restored muscle mass and function in aged mice, improved cardiac function while limiting adverse remodeling after myocardial infarction, and eased skeletal and cardiac muscle pathology in mouse and pig models of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Across those settings, inhibition turned on mitochondrial programs and suppressed inflammatory and fibrotic signaling, a pattern the authors liken to established longevity interventions. Separately, the miR-128-1 locus sits in a human haplotype on chromosome 2q21.3 that has been associated with grip strength, pulmonary function, and cardiometabolic traits; that is a genetic association, not a test of the drug. Elenae Therapeutics is developing the approach and, as described, is aimed first at more severe indications such as heart muscle after a heart attack. Source: [fightaging.org](https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/10/mir-128-3p-inhibition-improves-muscle-mass-and-function-in-aged-mice/)

### Mechanism of the Week: Sleep and Aging
In the Sleep Heart Health Study, 5,407 community-dwelling adults, mean age 63 and ranging from 45 to 99, with 52% women, showed poorer objectively measured sleep with older age even after chronic health conditions were taken into account. That cross-sectional study, published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society, used unattended home polysomnography plus questionnaires. It is the largest measurement set in this week’s sleep sources, and it is still a snapshot, not a trial of changing sleep.

Sleep architecture is the night’s sequence of stages, scored from the electroencephalogram. Stage N1 is light sleep. N2 carries sleep spindles, brief bursts of faster activity. N3 is slow-wave sleep, the deep stage with large slow waves. Rapid eye movement sleep is the stage in which most dreaming occurs and the cortex is highly active. A circadian clock times when sleep is likely. With healthy aging, a 2015 review in Current Topics in Behavioral Neurosciences describes less slow-wave sleep and less of its spectral power, fewer and smaller spindles, lower rapid-eye-movement density, smaller circadian amplitude, and a phase advance, meaning the clock runs earlier. Mild cognitive impairment brings further losses of sleep quality, slow-wave sleep, spindles, and the share of rapid eye movement sleep. Conversion to Alzheimer’s disease is described there as adding a profound disruption of circadian rhythmicity.

How those features relate to memory is still a set of associations. In younger adults, sleep-dependent consolidation is widely seen for both declarative and procedural tasks. The same review says that in healthy aging, consolidation of declarative memory is preserved, while some procedural tasks, including motor-sequence learning, do not show it. Fragmentation can reduce consolidation in younger adults, and a normal rise in fragmentation may account for part of the aging change. Specific features, spindles and slow-wave sleep, are strongly linked to consolidation, and both diminish with healthy aging and diminish further with mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer’s disease. That is a review of existing work, not a new experiment.

The Sleep Heart Health Study found that older age went with shorter sleep time, lower sleep efficiency, and more arousals in both men and women. In men, age was independently tied to more stage 1 and stage 2 sleep and less slow-wave and rapid eye movement sleep. In women the stage pattern was less strongly linear. Subjective complaints ran the other way by sex: poor subjective sleep was not tied to older age in men, while older women had more trouble falling asleep, with a trend toward more waking in the night and waking too early. Agreement between self-report and measured sleep time and sleep latency was low to moderate, with correlation coefficients from 0.06 to 0.32. A higher prevalence of chronic conditions, including sleep apnea, did not explain the age-related changes or the age-sex differences.

A 2022 systematic review in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health pooled 71 studies. Mean ages across samples ran from 58.3 to 93.7 years. Thirty-three studies used subjective measures, 31 used objective measures, and 10 used both. Pathological aging showed worse sleep than healthy older adults on both kinds of measure. In Alzheimer’s disease and mild cognitive impairment, the features most often compromised were rapid eye movement sleep, sleep efficiency, sleep latency, and sleep duration. The reviewers’ reading is that frequency and severity of sleep disturbance follow the evolution of cognitive impairment, and that objective measures look more consistent than subjective ones. A review synthesizes other studies; it does not assign cause.

A longitudinal cohort of men from the Metropolit 1953 Danish Male Birth Cohort, published in Sleep Medicine, tied baseline microstructure to cognition over about ten years. Cognitive testing was done in 2010–2013 and again in 2020–2022, with 206 men at baseline and 106 at follow-up. Polysomnography was baseline only, in 176 men, and spindle, slow-wave, and EEG-coherence analyses were limited to 82 men with adequate non-rapid-eye-movement sleep. Over ten years, Trail Making Test B slowed by 6.1 seconds and the Symbol Digit Modalities Test fell by 2.3 points. Higher sleep efficiency tracked better cognitive maintenance. More wake after sleep onset and a higher arousal index tracked poorer memory and learning. A higher share of N1 tracked poorer executive function, while N2 and N3 were positively associated with cognitive outcomes. Fast spindle amplitude and frequency, slow-wave characteristics, and N2 and rapid-eye-movement coherence correlated with processing speed, attention, and global cognition. Analyses used Spearman and partial Spearman correlations with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. The authors call the findings exploratory and say the predictive value for neurodegenerative disease is not established.

A smaller imaging study in Molecular Psychiatry tested a long-standing idea about rapid eye movement sleep. Twenty-four older adults without dementia, mean age 71.29 years, 58.33% women, and 25% with amnestic mild cognitive impairment, had in-laboratory polysomnography, neuropsychological testing, structural MRI, and PET with FEOBV, a tracer of brain cholinergic innervation. Cholinergic activity supports cortical activation in rapid eye movement sleep, when other transmitter systems are nearly silent. Higher rapid-eye-movement EEG slowing, the ratio of slower to faster power, over frontal, central, parietal, occipital, and temporal derivations was associated with cortical cholinergic denervation, notably in fronto-parietal areas and the medial temporal lobe, in voxel-wise regressions controlling for sex. In exploratory sex-stratified analyses adjusted for age, the link sat mainly in medial temporal regions in women and in neocortical regions in men. FEOBV uptake was higher in women than in men. The authors suggest global rapid-eye-movement slowing may be a sensitive marker of cholinergic denervation in people without dementia. That is a cross-sectional association in 24 people, not a diagnostic standard.

Two further reviews set limits rather than new measurements. The 2015 review notes that insomnia, obstructive sleep apnea, and narcolepsy can impair sleep-dependent consolidation without neurodegenerative change, and that sleep disorders become more common with normal aging and more common still with neurodegenerative disease. It also notes that rapid-eye-movement behavior disorder can presage Parkinson’s disease. A 2018 review in Sleep Medicine Reviews proposes that chronic low-grade inflammation, called inflammaging, may mediate links among impaired sleep, dysfunctional adiposity, and cognitive decline through neuroinflammation, with reciprocal ties to the circadian system and to hormone resistance. That paper is a model. It does not demonstrate the pathway in a new cohort.

What is not established is any of the causal steps a listener might want. These sources do not show that napping, short sleep, or a given stage causes dementia, and they do not test whether changing sleep changes cognitive trajectories. The strongest longitudinal microstructure result is in older men only, with microstructure data on 82 people, and its authors mark it as exploratory. Subjective and objective sleep disagree, and they disagree differently in men and women. No paper here evaluates a drug, a device, or a regulator decision about sleep as an aging treatment. The strongest finding’s limit is the Sleep Heart Health Study itself: age tracks worse measured sleep in thousands of adults, independent of the chronic conditions the investigators could account for, and that still does not say what would happen if sleep were changed.

### Worth Knowing
- An observational cohort found that frequent and unintentional daytime napping preceded many dementia diagnoses, which fits a marker of changing wakefulness at least as well as a cause.
- In healthy volunteers, cellular recycling did not show one age-related direction, so a blanket claim that autophagy simply fails with age is ahead of the human cell evidence.
- A congress comparison, not a randomized trial, found more nail disorders in GLP-1 users than in people with diabetes or obesity who had never used the drugs, beyond what weight loss alone explained in that report.
- Postmortem brain methylation tracked Alzheimer pathology and partly sat on the path from APOE genotype to diagnosis, which is a biological association, not a validated clinical clock.

### Evidence Ledger
- In 5,407 adults, older age tracked shorter sleep, lower efficiency, and more arousals on home polysomnography, independent of chronic conditions; evidence level: cross-sectional human study. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/18482295
- Across 71 studies, sleep disturbance was worse in pathological aging than in healthy older adults, and objective measures were more consistent than subjective ones; evidence level: systematic review. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/35886309
- In older Danish men, baseline spindles, slow waves, and EEG coherence correlated with ten-year cognitive change; evidence level: longitudinal observational cohort, exploratory. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42628340
- In 24 older adults without dementia, rapid-eye-movement EEG slowing tracked cortical cholinergic denervation on PET; evidence level: small cross-sectional human imaging study. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42120556
- Healthy aging brings less slow-wave sleep and fewer spindles, with further losses in mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer’s disease, and declarative sleep-dependent consolidation is described as preserved; evidence level: narrative review. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/24652608
- A proposed model links impaired sleep, adiposity, and cognitive decline through low-grade inflammation; evidence level: narrative review, not new data. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/30241997

This week’s clearest human findings are associations and early measurements, not treatments.

# Longevity Weekly
> **Eleven-gene reprogramming was given to people before any published human data.**

**What You Need to Know:** Eleven-gene reprogramming was given to people before any published human data, in an uncontrolled use that is not a clinical trial. Large observational cohorts, not experiments, again link cardiorespiratory fitness with later cardiovascular disease and death. A Greek criminal inquiry into a death at an anti-aging clinic has not established that plasmapheresis caused it.

### The Week in Longevity
**KHL Foundation Reports the Likely First Human Partial Epigenetic Reprogramming Treatments:** Fight Aging!
This is an uncontrolled, unpublished use, not a randomized human trial and not a peer-reviewed outcome study. Fight Aging! reports that partial epigenetic reprogramming with adeno-associated viral vectors was given to a small number of people through medical-tourism manufacture, including a Triple Helix Science initiative, and that this was not the first patient in Life Biosciences’ recently launched optic-neuropathy trial. The KHL Foundation, linked to Kenneth Scott (born 1942) and Helga Sands (born 1938), is described as adapting rejuvenation technologies for people who want them now. One recipient, Christine Scott, received an experimental therapy described as an 11-gene construct containing OCT4, SOX2, and KLF4 on March 11, 2026, given submucosally with cognition as the stated target, and with expression described as switched by a doxycycline activation approach. The same report says this corner of practice usually does not produce formally published data. No regulator approval for aging is described, and composition, safety, and effect are not established by a published human study. Source: [fightaging.org](https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/10/khl-foundation-reports-the-likely-first-human-partial-epigenetic-reprogramming-treatments/)

**Direct Pharmacological Activation of AMPK Modestly Extends Life in Short-Lived Species:** Fight Aging!
This is a preclinical study in short-lived species, not a human trial. Fight Aging! reports a paper in which the direct AMPK activator compound 991 extended lifespan in Drosophila melanogaster, Caenorhabditis elegans, and Schizosaccharomyces pombe, while in mice it induced what the authors call a pro-longevity proteomic profile rather than a reported lifespan gain. The commentary calls the lifespan effect modest and argues these species respond more readily to metabolic alteration than humans do. The same piece says metformin activates AMPK indirectly by shifting the cellular AMP/ADP:ATP ratio and that animal data on that indirect route are mixed. Nothing in the report is a human result, and no regulator approval of compound 991 for aging is described. Source: [fightaging.org](https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/10/direct-pharmacological-activation-of-ampk-modestly-extends-life-in-short-lived-species/)

**After Giorgos Mazonakis’s death, Greece weighs tighter rules for plasma exchange clinics and anti-aging claims:** Ecostylia
This is investigative reporting of a death and a criminal inquiry, not evidence that plasmapheresis slows aging or that it caused the death. Giorgos Mazonakis, 54, died on September 9, 2026, after a cardiac arrest at a Kolonaki clinic where he had an appointment for plasmapheresis offered as an anti-aging service; Elpis Hospital said he arrived at 4:45 p.m. with no spontaneous breathing or pulse and was pronounced dead at 5:40 p.m. The two doctors under investigation deny wrongdoing and say he lost consciousness before treatment; the outlet reports that investigators dispute that account. As of September 24 both were in pretrial detention on homicide charges, which does not establish guilt. On October 6 the family’s lawyer, Charalambos Lykoudis, said toxicology and histology results were still awaited. Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis said on September 9 that the facility’s internal-medicine license did not allow plasmapheresis, and the case prompted the government to announce a new regulatory framework for such centers. The outlet states that the sequence of an appointment and a cardiac arrest does not itself prove a causal link. Source: [ecostylia.com](https://www.ecostylia.com/en/mazonakis-death-clinic-antiaging/)

**Chronic Inflammation in the Aging of Bone and Brain Tissue:** Fight Aging!
This is a review framework, not a new human trial and not a measured treatment effect. Fight Aging! describes a paper that treats the correlation between osteoporosis and neurodegenerative disease as more likely to reflect shared upstream processes than one disease causing the other. The process it centers is inflammaging: a chronic, low-grade, sterile systemic inflammatory state driven by senescent cells and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. The review is presented as consolidating existing evidence into an immunopathological frame for bone and brain aging together. Source: [fightaging.org](https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/10/chronic-inflammation-in-the-aging-of-bone-and-brain-tissue/)

### Mechanism of the Week: Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Mortality
Directly measured maximal oxygen uptake, VO2max, during cardiopulmonary exercise testing is the gold-standard reading of cardiorespiratory fitness in this literature. A 2009 meta-analysis in JAMA expressed that capacity as maximal aerobic capacity in metabolic equivalents and treated one metabolic equivalent as corresponding to about one kilometre per hour higher running or jogging speed. Newer cohorts often estimate the same idea instead of measuring gases. One 2026 UK Biobank analysis used submaximal cycle ergometry. A companion 2026 paper estimated fitness from the heart-rate response to incremental workload on a risk-stratified submaximal test. A reported fitness number may therefore be a laboratory maximum or a calculation.

These papers do not establish one molecular switch. A 2010 review says several biological mechanisms suggest that fitness improves insulin sensitivity, blood lipids, body composition, inflammation, and blood pressure. That is a review of proposed links, not an experiment that isolated a path. A 2026 observational molecular study found higher fitness characterized by lower pathway signals for inflammation, triglyceride metabolism, glycolysis, and vascular dysfunction, and higher signals for cholesterol transport, apolipoprotein particle size, and cytoskeletal remodeling. Those are circulating associations. They are not proof that changing one protein changes lifespan.

The strongest human evidence is prospective and observational. The 2009 JAMA meta-analysis pooled 33 cohorts: 102,980 participants and 6,910 deaths for all-cause mortality, and 84,323 participants and 4,485 cases for coronary or cardiovascular events. Each 1-MET higher maximal aerobic capacity was associated with a relative risk of 0.87 for all-cause death (95% confidence interval 0.84 to 0.90) and 0.85 for those events (0.82 to 0.88). Low versus high fitness carried a relative risk of 1.70 for all-cause death (1.51 to 1.92). Participants at 7.9 METs or more had substantially lower rates of all-cause death and of those events than people below 7.9 METs. A 2015 meta-analysis in Annals of Oncology, six prospective studies, 71,654 people and 2,002 cancer deaths, median follow-up 16.4 years, found a graded inverse association with total cancer mortality. Versus low fitness, intermediate fitness had a summary relative risk of 0.80 (0.67 to 0.97) and high fitness 0.55 (0.47 to 0.65). Studies that adjusted for adiposity looked similar to those that did not. A 2017 review says that inverse pattern persisted across a decade even when methods ranged from directly measured VO2max to exercise-test estimates and non-exercise equations, and it notes that the American Heart Association had advocated routine fitness assessment as a clinical vital sign. That is a professional-society position in a review, not a drug approval.

A 1996 JAMA clinic cohort used a maximal exercise test in 25,341 men and 7,080 women: 601 deaths in 211,996 man-years and 89 deaths in 52,982 woman-years. Low fitness remained an independent predictor, adjusted relative risk 1.52 in men (1.28 to 1.82) and 2.10 in women (1.36 to 3.21). In women the other statistically significant independent predictor reported was smoking, relative risk 1.99 (1.25 to 3.17). Inverse gradients held inside strata of smoking, cholesterol, blood pressure, and health status. Fit people with any combination of smoking, elevated blood pressure, or elevated cholesterol had lower adjusted death rates than low-fit people with none of those traits. A 2010 review says prior studies find that fitness appears to attenuate the higher death risk associated with obesity. None of these cohorts randomized people to a fitness level.

Two 2026 UK Biobank analyses ask whether change, and whether a blood signature of fitness, still track later disease. In 11,530 participants aged 40 to 73 with two submaximal assessments, prior cardiovascular disease excluded, and events within two years of follow-up excluded, Cox models adjusted for baseline fitness, sociodemographic and lifestyle factors, genetic predisposition to cardiovascular disease, body-mass-index change, and physical activity. Median follow-up was 14.0 years (interquartile range 13.0 to 14.6), with 921 incident cardiovascular events and 119 cardiovascular deaths. Each additional 1 mL·kg−1·min−1·year−1 of estimated VO2max was associated with a hazard ratio of 0.85 for incident disease (0.75 to 0.96) and 0.66 for cardiovascular death (0.51 to 0.87). The authors describe an approximately linear pattern without a threshold; declines were associated with higher risk. Metabolomic and proteomic signatures built from the submaximal test reflected fitness with an R-squared of about 0.50 to 0.60 and were checked in 354,222 people with metabolomics and 29,961 with proteomics. Over an average of nine years, 27,659 all-cause deaths occurred. The metabolomic signature was associated with a 39 to 54 percent lower risk of all-cause death, a 90 percent lower risk of type 2 diabetes in both discovery and validation, a 42 to 47 percent lower cardiovascular risk, and a 33 to 39 percent lower colorectal-cancer risk. The proteomic signature was associated with a 17 percent lower risk of all-cause death and a 22 to 39 percent lower risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, after adjustment for age, sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, smoking, alcohol, diet, body mass index, and relevant medical history.

Cause is not established. Illness can lower a fitness score and raise risk together. An estimate is not a gas-measured maximum. A signature is not itself an outcome, and the outcome links remain associations. Intervals on rarer deaths are wide. These papers do not report a regulator approving fitness testing, or exercise, as a treatment for aging. The limit on the newest result is the limit on the older ones: after baseline fitness is already in the model, a yearly rise of 1 mL/kg/min in estimated VO2max still lines up with lower cardiovascular risk, and that lineup does not show that producing the rise will produce the drop.

### Worth Knowing
- A fitness change that still tracks with later cardiovascular disease in an observational cohort, after starting fitness is already accounted for, is a sharper description than a one-time label, and it is still not proof of cause.
- Lower cancer mortality in higher fitness categories, across prospective observational studies, does not separate fitness itself from the rest of the life that produces the score.
- An anti-aging clinic appointment and a cardiac arrest the same afternoon, in investigative reporting, do not establish what the procedure did.

### Evidence Ledger
- Directly measured VO2max is described as the gold-standard fitness method, and the American Heart Association had advocated routine assessment as a clinical vital sign; evidence level: review. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/28286137
- Each 1-MET higher maximal aerobic capacity was associated with lower all-cause and coronary or cardiovascular risk in pooled observational cohorts; evidence level: meta-analysis of cohorts. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/19454641
- Higher cardiorespiratory fitness was associated with lower total cancer mortality in six prospective studies; evidence level: meta-analysis of observational studies. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/25009011
- Low fitness independently predicted death in a preventive-clinic cohort of men and women who completed a maximal exercise test; evidence level: observational cohort. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/8667564
- Reviews summarize fitness as a strong mortality predictor and list proposed links through insulin sensitivity, lipids, body composition, inflammation, and blood pressure; evidence level: review. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/20923918
- Annual change in estimated VO2max predicted incident cardiovascular disease and cardiovascular death beyond baseline fitness in UK Biobank; evidence level: observational cohort. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42605962
- Metabolomic and proteomic signatures of fitness were associated with later death and noncommunicable disease in UK Biobank; evidence level: observational cohort. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42394615

### Trial Tracker
- Life Biosciences optic-neuropathy trial: partial epigenetic reprogramming, described as recently launched; no next dated milestone is named in this week’s sources.
- Targeting Aging with Metformin (TAME): metformin, followed as a proposed aging-indication trial; no new phase, enrolment figure, or dated milestone is in this week’s sources.

A treatment given to a person is not a result until a study measures one.

# Longevity Weekly
> **Fourteen randomized trials showed resistance training raised handgrip strength in older adults with sarcopenia.**

**What You Need to Know:** Human randomized trials and meta-analyses demonstrate that resistance training improves muscle strength and physical performance measures such as gait speed in older adults with sarcopenia. These effects appear in both early and later stages of frailty. No regulator has approved any specific resistance training protocol for aging-related indications.

### The Week in Longevity
**Exercise slowed epigenetic aging in breast cancer survivors RCT:** A randomized controlled trial found that exercise slowed epigenetic aging among breast cancer survivors. The result comes from a human trial published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute. The trial measured epigenetic age markers before and after the exercise intervention in this specific population. Source: [academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/jnci/advance-article/doi/10.1093/jnci/djag296/8845541?searchresult=1)

**Retatrutide RCT for obesity published in NEJM:** The retatrutide randomized clinical trial for obesity, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, reported up to 30 percent loss of body weight versus placebo. Retatrutide is a triple receptor agonist acting on GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors. The trial confirmed marked potency of this triple receptor GLP-1 drug in participants with obesity. Source: [nejm.org](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2604169?query=featured_home)

**Exercise New Zealand spotlights research on muscle power’s association with longevity:** Exercise New Zealand highlighted observational research linking greater muscle power to longevity outcomes. The association rests on measures of physical function in older adults. The spotlight draws attention to how muscle power correlates with survival and independence measures. Source: [ausleisure.com.au](https://www.ausleisure.com.au/news/exercise-new-zealand-spotlights-research-on-muscle-powers-association-with-longevity)

**Regular Daily Routines Tied to Less Pain and Depression in Older Adults:** Observational data linked regular daily routines to lower levels of pain and depression in older adults. The finding comes from a cross-sectional analysis of routine stability. Participants with more consistent daily patterns showed reduced symptom scores on standardized assessments. Source: [thewellnews.com](https://www.thewellnews.com/health/regular-daily-routines-tied-to-less-pain-and-depression-in-older-adults/)

### Mechanism of the Week: Muscle, Strength and Aging
This week's mechanism examines how resistance training and related interventions influence sarcopenia and physical function in older adults. Sarcopenia describes the progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength and physical function that occurs with advancing age and raises risks of frailty, falls and loss of independence. In one randomized controlled trial, sixty-eight community-dwelling older adults aged sixty-seven point two years on average with hamstring tightness and possible sarcopenia were randomly assigned to high-volume static stretching for thirty minutes daily, low-volume static stretching for three minutes three days per week, eccentric exercise or a non-intervention control for six weeks. Assessments conducted at baseline, post-intervention and three-month follow-up included muscle thickness, range of motion, musculotendinous unit stiffness, isometric knee flexor strength, cross-education effects on contralateral strength, Y-Balance performance and function outcomes. Significant group by time interaction effects were observed for range of motion and isometric strength. Eccentric exercise improved strength more than the control condition, whereas stretching-related changes remained below the minimal detectable change. No statistically detectable difference in range of motion was identified between high- and low-volume stretching. Low-volume stretching required substantially less weekly exercise time than high-volume stretching. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of fourteen randomized controlled trials in healthy older adults with sarcopenia found resistance training produced a standardized mean difference of zero point eight one for handgrip strength, one point two six for knee extension strength, one point two eight for gait speed and minus zero point nine three for the timed up and go test. A separate 2021 meta-analysis of twenty-five randomized trials with two thousand two hundred sixty-seven participants reported benefits on handgrip strength with an effect size of zero point five one, lower-limb strength with an effect size of zero point nine three, gait speed with an effect size of zero point seven five, functional performance with an effect size of zero point seven six and muscle mass with an effect size of zero point two nine. Resistance training during early stages had positive effects in all variables, being particularly effective in improving gait speed with an effect size of zero point six three and functional strength with an effect size of zero point five three. The PROVIDE study, a multicenter randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of three hundred eighty sarcopenic primarily independent-living older adults, showed that a vitamin D and leucine-enriched whey protein nutritional supplement taken twice daily for thirteen weeks improved chair-stand time by one point zero one seconds and appendicular muscle mass by zero point one seven kilograms compared with an iso-caloric control. One meta-analysis found no statistically significant effect on appendicular skeletal muscle mass or skeletal muscle mass overall. No regulator has approved resistance training as a therapy for aging-related muscle loss. The effects on muscle mass were not consistent across studies. The mechanism acts on the hallmark of altered intercellular communication. The PROVIDE study was a completed randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial.

### Worth Knowing
- Randomized trials establish that resistance training improves strength and gait speed in older adults diagnosed with sarcopenia.
- Meta-analyses of human data show these strength gains occur in both early prevention and later treatment stages of frailty.
- Observational evidence connects higher muscle power to longevity, consistent with trial findings on physical performance.

### Evidence Ledger
- Resistance training produced a standardized mean difference of 0.81 for handgrip strength in a meta-analysis of fourteen randomized trials; evidence level is randomized human trial; source https://europepmc.org/article/MED/34763651.
- Resistance training improved handgrip strength with effect size 0.51 and lower-limb strength with effect size 0.93 across twenty-five randomized trials; evidence level is randomized human trial; source https://europepmc.org/article/MED/33921356.
- A vitamin D and leucine-enriched whey protein supplement improved chair-stand performance and appendicular muscle mass in a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 380 sarcopenic adults; evidence level is randomized human trial; source https://europepmc.org/article/MED/26170041.

### Trial Tracker
- PROVIDE study: vitamin D and leucine-enriched whey protein supplement versus iso-caloric control; randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial completed; no further dated milestone named in sources.

This is Longevity Weekly for September 30, 2026.

# Longevity Weekly
> **Phase 3 trials showed positive results for an autoimmune drug, an obesity maintenance regimen, and a gene therapy for a rare eye disease.**

**What You Need to Know:** This edition covers recent human trial results in autoimmune disease, obesity, and inherited eye conditions, plus observational data on cardiovascular health and insomnia treatment. It also introduces the hallmarks of aging framework used throughout the series to classify biological findings by evidence level. All reporting stays within published sources and states the type of evidence for each claim.

### What This Show Covers
The science of aging examines measurable biological processes that change over time and contribute to disease risk. The hallmarks framework organizes these processes into categories such as genomic instability, telomere attrition, epigenetic alterations, loss of proteostasis, disabled macroautophagy, deregulated nutrient-sensing, mitochondrial dysfunction, cellular senescence, stem cell exhaustion, altered intercellular communication, chronic inflammation, and dysbiosis. This episode uses the framework as its first worked example to separate cell or animal data from human outcomes and to note what remains untested in people. The show presents education only and never medical advice; every finding is labeled by evidence level so a mouse result is never presented as a human result. Longevity Weekly is part of the Nerra Network, an independent network of shows at nerranetwork.com. Listeners can find the full archive and related programs at that site.

### The Week in Longevity
**Amgen reports a Phase 3 win with Sjögren’s drug candidate: BioPharma Dive**
Dazodalibep met its primary endpoint in one of two late-stage randomized human trials for Sjögren’s syndrome, an autoimmune disorder. The result comes from a Phase 3 study conducted after Amgen acquired the asset through its purchase of Horizon Therapeutics. The candidate targets the tough-to-treat condition via a mechanism acquired in the Horizon buyout. The trial represents the first of two planned late-stage studies. No regulatory decision on an aging-related indication has been reported. Source: [biopharmadive.com](https://www.biopharmadive.com/news/amgen-dazodalibep-sjogrens-syndrome-study-results/831042/)

**Viking shares surge on updated obesity drug data: BioPharma Dive**
Participants in a randomized human trial maintained weight loss after switching from weekly to less frequent dosing of the company’s obesity drug. The maintenance data come from a late-stage study and were described by one analyst as strengthening competitive positioning. Trial participants largely sustained the weight reduction achieved on the initial weekly regimen. The findings address questions around dosing frequency in ongoing obesity treatment. No approval for aging-related use has been granted. Source: [biopharmadive.com](https://www.biopharmadive.com/news/viking-obesity-drug-maintenance-study-results/831004/)

**Beacon eye gene therapy hits mark in late-stage study: BioPharma Dive**
A pivotal randomized trial of the gene therapy laru-zova met its primary endpoint in patients with X-linked retinitis pigmentosa. The result marks the first time a treatment for this inherited retinal condition achieved its main goal in a Phase 3 study. The trial evaluated the therapy in a population with the rare and potentially blinding disorder. Beacon presented the data as meeting the study’s primary objective. Regulatory review status has not been detailed in the report. Source: [biopharmadive.com](https://www.biopharmadive.com/news/beacon-xlrp-laru-zova-phase-3-study-results/830918/)

**Intermittent Fasting Shows Promise in a Huntington’s Trial: Lifespan.io**
A small pilot randomized human study found that intermittent fasting produced measurable improvements in patients with Huntington’s disease. The authors noted the limited sample size and called for larger trials before drawing firm conclusions. The pilot examined patients with this inherited neurodegenerative condition currently considered untreatable. Improvements were observed in disease-related measures during the fasting intervention. No regulatory body has approved intermittent fasting for this or any aging indication. Source: [lifespan.io](https://lifespan.io/intermittent-fasting-shows-promise-in-a-huntingtons-trial/)

**Treating insomnia with CBT-I may slow biological aging in older adults: Medical News Today**
An observational analysis linked cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia to slower epigenetic aging markers in older adults. The finding rests on biomarker associations rather than direct clinical outcomes and requires further randomized confirmation. The study examined older adults receiving CBT-I as treatment for insomnia. Epigenetic clocks served as the measure of biological aging change. Source: [medicalnewstoday.com](https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/could-treating-insomnia-slow-biological-aging-study-finds-promising-link)

**Low Cardiovascular Risk in Early Midlife Correlates with Better Late Life Health: Fight Aging!**
Longitudinal observational data from several thousand participants showed that lower cardiovascular risk in the early forties correlated with reduced frailty and higher odds of reaching age 90. The spread in survival outcomes between lowest- and highest-risk groups reached six-fold in some metrics. The analysis processed data from a long-running study of midlife cardiovascular profiles. Researchers tracked frailty, quality of life, happiness, and well-being measures into old age. The analysis does not establish causation. Source: [fightaging.org](https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/09/low-cardiovascular-risk-in-early-midlife-correlates-with-better-late-life-health/)

### Mechanism of the Week: The Hallmarks of Aging
The hallmarks of aging are a set of twelve biological processes whose age-associated changes meet three criteria: they appear with advancing age, their experimental accentuation speeds aging, and their therapeutic targeting can slow, stop, or reverse aspects of aging in model systems. The original nine hallmarks were proposed in 2013 and later expanded to twelve to include disabled macroautophagy, chronic inflammation, and dysbiosis. Each hallmark describes a distinct but interconnected layer of cellular and tissue decline. Genomic instability refers to the accumulation of DNA damage and mutations; telomere attrition shortens chromosome ends and triggers DNA damage responses; epigenetic alterations change gene expression patterns without altering DNA sequence; loss of proteostasis impairs protein folding and clearance; disabled macroautophagy reduces the cell’s ability to recycle damaged components; deregulated nutrient-sensing disrupts pathways such as mTOR and AMPK that normally adjust metabolism to nutrient availability; mitochondrial dysfunction lowers energy production and increases reactive oxygen species; cellular senescence causes cells to stop dividing and secrete inflammatory signals; stem cell exhaustion depletes the pool of cells needed for tissue repair; altered intercellular communication changes signaling between cells; chronic inflammation sustains low-grade immune activation; and dysbiosis alters microbial communities that influence host metabolism and immunity. Evidence for the framework itself derives from reviews that compile cell, animal, and limited human observations rather than from any single randomized trial. The 2013 Cell paper enumerated the initial nine hallmarks and the 2023 update added three more while retaining the same three-premise test for inclusion. A 2020 review examined how metformin interacts with several hallmarks in cell and animal models, showing improvements in nutrient sensing, autophagy, and intercellular communication, yet noted that human outcome data remain limited to the ongoing TAME trial whose results are not yet available. Telomere studies illustrate how one hallmark can intersect with others, amplifying DNA damage responses and senescence, but these links rest primarily on cell and animal experiments. What is not established is whether intervening on any single hallmark produces consistent, clinically meaningful extension of healthy lifespan in humans; no hallmark-targeted therapy has received regulatory approval for an aging indication. Known risks of experimental interventions include off-target effects on cell proliferation or immune function, though specific safety profiles vary by agent and remain under study.

### Evidence Ledger
- The twelve hallmarks satisfy three premises of age association, experimental acceleration, and potential therapeutic reversal, as stated in a 2023 review. Evidence level: literature synthesis. Source: [europepmc.org](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/36599349)
- Metformin attenuates multiple hallmarks including nutrient sensing, autophagy, and intercellular communication in cell and animal models. Evidence level: cell and animal studies. Source: [europepmc.org](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/32333835)
- The original nine hallmarks were defined by the same three premises in a 2013 review. Evidence level: literature synthesis. Source: [europepmc.org](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/23746838)

### Trial Tracker
- TAME (Targeting Aging with Metformin): metformin, Phase 3 planning stage; next milestone not dated in sources.
- Viking obesity maintenance trial: unnamed obesity drug, late-stage; weight maintenance data reported.
- Beacon XLRP trial: laru-zova gene therapy, Phase 3; primary endpoint met.
- Huntington’s intermittent fasting pilot: intermittent fasting, pilot randomized; improvements observed, larger trials requested.

This episode marks the debut of Longevity Weekly.
